name: Dave Thomas
milestone_by_age_26: Major recognition arrived with co-authoring The Pragmatic Programmer (1999) at about age 39 and the Agile Manifesto (2001) at about age 41; no specific dated material milestone by age 26 found.
early_history_summary: British-born programmer who studied computer science at Imperial College London, later moved to the US (1994), and became known for Ruby advocacy, the DRY principle, code katas, and co-founding The Pragmatic Bookshelf.
evidence_summary: Wikipedia and secondary profiles place birth around 1960 (category conflict notes 1956 on one wiki listing). His signature achievements—The Pragmatic Programmer (1999), Programming Ruby (2000), Agile Manifesto signatory (2001), Pragmatic Bookshelf—occurred in his late 30s and beyond. No independently dated material founder or product milestone by age 26 was verified.

name: Mike Engelhardt
milestone_by_age_26: No confirmed birth year in reviewed sources; cannot verify age at early simulator work (claimed since 1975) or at LTspice/QSPICE milestones. Without birth year, age-26 eligibility cannot be established.
early_history_summary: American physicist/programmer known for LTspice and later QSPICE. BS Physics University of Michigan (1981), MS Physics UC Berkeley (1983); long career writing analog circuit simulators including SwitcherCAD/LTspice at Linear Technology.
evidence_summary: Wikipedia marks year of birth missing. Degrees in 1981/1983 and industry fame via LTspice (public SwitcherCAD III ~1999; LTspice IV 2008) and QSPICE (2023) cannot be age-dated without a birth year. Self-reported simulator work since 1975 is not independently age-verified.

name: Alan Cooper
milestone_by_age_26: In 1975 at age 22–23, founded Structured Systems Group (SSG) in Oakland and shipped General Ledger, widely cited as among the first serious business software packages for microcomputers.
early_history_summary: Born in San Francisco (1952) and raised in Marin County; dropped out of high school, studied architecture at College of Marin while doing contract programming. As microcomputers arrived he founded SSG (1975), published General Ledger via Byte/Interface Age ads, co-worked on CBASIC with Gordon Eubanks, later joined Digital Research briefly, then built SuperProject and the Ruby visual programming work that became Visual Basic.
family_context_summary: Raised in Marin County after family moved from San Francisco when he was about four; detailed parental occupations and wealth not documented in reviewed sources.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources as a software/industry apprenticeship path.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Bay Area microcomputers, early PC software market, self-taught programming, SSG founding, CBASIC/DRI network
evidence_summary: Cooper founded one of the first microcomputer software companies at ~23 and sold General Ledger as serious business software on early micros—dated and corroborated via Wikipedia and Fire in the Valley / industry histories. Bay Area geography and hands-on customer/product work were clear advantages; family capital and elite-institution pipelines are not documented. Later work (Ruby → Visual Basic, personas, interaction design firm) cemented tier-2 historical status.
starting_point: Born 1952 in San Francisco; raised in Marin County; rebellious high-school dropout path into College of Marin architecture study funded by contract programming.
current_position: Interaction design pioneer and CHM Fellow; firm Cooper was acquired into Designit/Wipro Digital (2017); continues as a recognized father of Visual Basic and personas methodology.

trajectory.event: Founded Structured Systems Group and released General Ledger, among the first serious business applications for microcomputers.
Sold his interest in Structured Systems Group after shipping roughly a dozen original products.
Sold SuperProject critical-path project management software to Computer Associates.
Built Ruby visual shell construction set, which Microsoft acquired and evolved into Visual Basic.
Co-founded Cooper interaction design consultancy with Sue Cooper.
Published About Face, establishing core interaction-design principles later revised through multiple editions.
Inducted into the Computer History Museum Hall of Fellows for Visual Basic and interaction design pioneering work.

name: Mary Blue
milestone_by_age_26: No confirmed birth year; BA 1977 and PhD 1982 form a standard academic path without a dated exceptional material milestone verifiable by age 26.
early_history_summary: American neurobiologist; BA biology Cornell College (1977), PhD cell biology UTHealth (1982), postdoc Johns Hopkins, then research scientist at Kennedy Krieger and associate professor of neurology/neuroscience at Johns Hopkins.
evidence_summary: Wikipedia biography lacks birth year. Documented milestones (BA 1977, PhD 1982, Kennedy Krieger/JHU faculty track from 1989) do not establish a specific material breakout by age 26 without birth-year confirmation, and the path appears conventional academic progression rather than a dated founder/breakthrough event.

name: Ray Ozzie
milestone_by_age_26: Career-defining milestones came after 26: left Lotus to found Iris Associates in 1984 (age ~28–29) and Lotus Notes shipped commercially around 1989 after development completion ~1986 (age ~30–31). Pre-26 work (UIUC/PLATO, Data General, Software Arts) was strong employment, not a dated personal breakthrough product/founding event.
early_history_summary: Born Chicago 1955; learned programming in high school; BS CS University of Illinois 1979 working on PLATO; early career at Data General and Software Arts (VisiCalc/TK Solver), then Lotus Symphony, then Iris Associates for Notes.
family_context_summary: Grew up in Chicago/Park Ridge, Illinois; family financial/domain details not richly documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: By age 26 (Nov 1981) Ozzie had graduated UIUC and held roles at Data General and Software Arts—impressive apprenticeship, but the material founder/product milestone (Iris Associates / Lotus Notes) is solidly post-26. Conservative eligibility rule does not credit later fame retroactively.

name: Charles Best
milestone_by_age_26: In 2000 at about age 24, founded DonorsChoose while teaching history at a Bronx public high school, creating an early education crowdfunding platform for classroom project requests.
early_history_summary: Attended St. Paul's School (NH), graduated Phi Beta Kappa from Yale College in 1998, then taught high school history in the Bronx. Two years after graduation he launched DonorsChoose from his classroom; students initially helped staff the operation. The model scaled nationally and pioneered teacher-directed crowdfunding.
family_context_summary: Elite prep school (St. Paul's) and Yale path imply substantial educational privilege; specific parental occupations and wealth not detailed in reviewed sources.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented as education-tech or nonprofit-domain family apprenticeship in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: St. Paul's, Yale, Bronx classroom immersion, early web crowdfunding, teacher-domain exposure
evidence_summary: Multiple independent bios state he launched DonorsChoose in 2000 as a ~24-year-old Bronx teacher after Yale 1998—matching birth year ~1976. Direct classroom problem exposure drove product design; elite education pipeline is clear. Family domain/network advantages beyond schooling are not well documented. Platform later became a major education nonprofit; he later led Lakeshore Learning.
starting_point: Elite U.S. prep (St. Paul's School) and Yale Phi Beta Kappa graduate (1998); entered public-school teaching in the Bronx rather than a conventional finance/consulting path.
current_position: Founder of DonorsChoose; became CEO of Lakeshore Learning (education supply retail) around 2023; prominent education philanthropy and social entrepreneurship figure.

trajectory.event: Graduated Phi Beta Kappa from Yale College and soon began teaching history in a Bronx public high school.
Founded DonorsChoose from his classroom, enabling teachers to post classroom project needs for public crowdfunding.
Named an Ashoka Fellow for social entrepreneurship innovation in education philanthropy.
DonorsChoose named one of Oprah Winfrey's Ultimate Favorite Things, accelerating national visibility.
Received the John F. Kennedy New Frontier Award for public service by young Americans.
Became CEO of Lakeshore Learning Materials, expanding from nonprofit crowdfunding into education retail leadership.

name: Sebastian Ruder
milestone_by_age_26: No confirmed birth year found; finished undergrad around 2015 and PhD ~2015–2019 with research roles at AYLIEN then DeepMind/Meta. Without birth year, material milestones cannot be age-verified by 26.
early_history_summary: Computational linguistics background (Heidelberg, Trinity College Dublin); PhD on transfer learning for NLP while research scientist at AYLIEN; later DeepMind and Meta research scientist known for multilingual NLP and accessible NLP writing.
evidence_summary: Public CV/about pages do not state birth year. Notable industry research posts (DeepMind, Meta, Cohere) and PhD completion are not age-dated. Conservative rule: ineligible without verifiable age-at-milestone.

name: Garry Tan
milestone_by_age_26: In September 2005 at about age 24, joined Palantir Technologies as employee #10, designing the company logo and cofounding early product/engineering work on its quant finance analysis platform.
early_history_summary: Born 1981 in Winnipeg to a Chinese Singaporean father (machine-shop foreman) and Burmese Chinese mother (nursing assistant); family moved to Fremont, CA in 1991. Began programming at 14, cold-called for early coding work. BS computer systems engineering Stanford (1999–2003), Microsoft, then Palantir #10 (2005–2007), then co-founded Posterous (YC S08).
family_context_summary: Immigrant working-class parents (machine-shop foreman father; nursing-assistant mother); not born wealthy; family relocated from Canada to Fremont, California in 1991.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were not software/VC domain experts; father worked in a machine shop and mother as a nursing assistant—no direct tech apprenticeship documented.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Stanford, Bay Area, Palantir early employee, Posterous/YC, design-engineering hybrid
evidence_summary: Birth year 1981 and Palantir tenure from Sep 2005 (LinkedIn + multiple profiles) place him at ~24 as employee #10 with logo and product founding contributions—material early-career milestone comparable to other FE-batch early unicorn hires. Working-class immigrant family background contrasts with Stanford/Bay Area institutional acceleration. Later co-founded Posterous (acquired by Twitter), Initialized Capital, and became YC president/CEO.
starting_point: Born 1981 in Winnipeg to immigrant working-class parents (machine-shop foreman and nursing assistant); family settled in Fremont, California in 1991; self-taught programming from age 14.
current_position: President and CEO of Y Combinator (since 2023) and board partner/advisor at Initialized Capital; active San Francisco tech and politics figure.

trajectory.event: Graduated Stanford with a BS in computer systems engineering and began professional work including Microsoft.
Joined Palantir as employee #10; designed the logo and helped build early quant finance analysis product/engineering.
Co-founded Posterous (YC S08), a blogging platform later acquired by Twitter (~$20M, 2012).
Joined Y Combinator as designer-in-residence and partner after leaving Posterous.
Co-founded Initialized Capital with partners including Alexis Ohanian; wrote early Coinbase seed check.
Became president and CEO of Y Combinator, returning to lead the accelerator.

name: James Allchin
category: Microsoft platforms executive, systems software engineer
milestone_by_age_26: Career-defining work came after 26: Stanford MS (1980, age ~29), Georgia Tech PhD/Clouds OS work early 1980s, Banyan VINES architecture from 1983 (age ~32), Microsoft from 1990 (age ~39). Pre-26 path (UF BS 1973, TI OS work, early companies with Dick Kiger) is solid engineering employment without a clearly dated breakout product of lasting fame by 26.
early_history_summary: Born Grand Rapids 1951; raised on Florida citrus farm; BS Computer Science University of Florida 1973 after a music detour; TI OS work and early startups; later Stanford MS, Georgia Tech PhD, Banyan VINES CTO path, then Microsoft platforms leadership through Windows XP/Vista era.
family_context_summary: Working-class farm family in Keysville, Florida; parents worked citrus farm; neither parent attended college.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were citrus farmers, not computer scientists; no domain apprenticeship.
evidence_summary: Born 1951; age 26 falls in ~1977 when he was in early industry/startup roles after a 1973 BS—not the historical milestones (VINES, Microsoft Windows leadership) that define his reputation. Strict age-26 bar not met by a dated material breakthrough.

early_history_summary: Raised in Kharkiv, Ukraine; coded from childhood; applied math/CS degrees at Kharkiv Polytechnic; Google researcher contributing to TensorFlow/NLP; co-author of the 2017 Transformer paper; co-founded NEAR Protocol/NEAR AI.
family_context_summary: Grew up in Ukraine in the 1990s amid economic instability; detailed family occupations not documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Public sources confirm Ukraine upbringing, Kharkiv education, Google (~2014), Transformer paper (2017), and NEAR founding—none of which land at or before age 26 under the 1985 birth-year hypothesis used in candidate metadata. Exact birth year is weakly sourced publicly, but even under that assumption fame-defining work is later.
